Phosphine-catalysed (4+1) annulations
of b0-acetoxy allenoate with b,c-unsaturated
carbonyl compounds †
Yueqi Zhang, Danfeng Wang and Xiaofeng Tong
 *
While b,c-unsaturated carbonyl compounds have been widely used
as cC- or aC-nucleophiles, their potential aC,aC-bisnucleophilic
reactivity is still underdeveloped. Herein, a phosphine-catalysed
(4+1) annulation of b
0-acetoxy allenoate and a b,c-unsaturated
carbonyl compound is reported, wherein b0-acetoxy allenoate is
the 1,4-biselectrophilic component while the b,c-unsaturated car-
bonyl compound serves as an aC,aC-bisnucleophile. The process
not only provides a new reaction mode of b,c-unsaturated carbonyl
compounds under mild conditions but also broadens the scope of
Lewis base-catalysed annulation of acetoxy allenoate.
The addition of dienolate to various electrophiles is a useful process
to forge C–C and C–N bonds. 1 In this context, b,g-unsaturated
carbonyl compounds1 are particularly attractive since the presence
of such two functional groups renders the aC–H higher activity,2
being amenable to generate dienolate speciesA under mild condi-
tions (Scheme 1a). For such species, two divergent addition path-
ways have been achieved, one is the vinylogous nucleophilic
addition of gC to various electrophiles, such as carbonyl com-
pounds, imines and Michael acceptors;
3 the other is the addition to
aC albeit with relatively less competitiveness, which may be
ascribed to the fact that switching the reactive site from thegCt o
the aC requires the disruption of thep-conjugation system inherent
to the dienolate.4 Inspired by these well-known reports, it is logical
to postulate that the specific b,g-unsaturated carbonyl structure
remaining in the resulting a-addition product would allow for
further addition. However, this proposed twofold addition would
become, if possible, extremely difficult likely due to the increased
steric hindrance and thus harsh conditions might be unavoidable
(Scheme 1a).
5 We envisioned that utility of a highly reactive
1,n-biselectrophile might impart the second addition much higher
efficiency in the intramolecular fashion, achieving a novel (3+ n)
and/or (1+ n) annulation protocol between the b,g-unsaturated
carbonyl compound and 1,n-biselectrophile under mild conditions
(Scheme 1a).
Our group realized the phosphine-catalysed annulation of
b0-acetoxy allenoate 2 in 2010. 6 Since then, the annulations of
actoxy allenoates under Lewis base catalysis have been extensively
studied by several groups.
7 The key to these successes is the
involvement of 1,4-biselectrophilic diene-phosphonium speciesB
(Scheme 1b), 6,7 which is in sharp contrast to traditional
phosphine-catalysed annulations relying on the phosphonium-
carbanion zwitterion.
8 With these considerations in mind, we

hypothesized that a Michael-type addition of A to B would be
feasible to generate zwitterion C. More importantly, this in situ
generated speciesC m i g h tb ea b l et os e r v ea sab a s et oe n f o r c et h e
generation of dienolate D, which was able to trigger a second
intramolecular addition to furnish an annulation process. Herein,
we report the phosphine-catalysed (4+1) annulation of 1 and
2, which would not only provide a new reaction mode of
b,g-unsaturated carbonyl compounds under mild conditions but
also broaden the scope of Lewis base-catalysed annulation of
allenoate 2 (Scheme 1b).
To verify our hypothesis, we conducted the reaction of
b,g-unsaturated carbonyl compound 1a and allenoate 2 in
toluene at room temperature with the use of PPh
3 (20 mol%)
as a catalyst and Na 2CO3 as a base additive, which indeed
aﬀorded a (4+1) annulation product 3a albeit only in 30% yield
(Table 1, entry 1). When electron-richer phosphine catalysts,
such as PPh
2Me and PPhMe2, were instead employed under the
otherwise identical conditions, product 3a was isolated in 55%
and 41% yield, respectively (Table 1, entries 2 and 3). These
results implied that the electronic character of phosphine
played an important role in the reaction eﬃciency. While much
more electron-rich P
nBu3 gave product 3a in 28% yield, the use
of P(p-MeO–C6H4)3 improved the yield to 71% (Table 1, entries
4 and 5). As expected, either less electron-rich P( p-Me–C6H4)3
or electron-poor P( p-F–C6H4)3 was found to be inferior to
P(p-MeO–C6H4)3 (Table 1, entries 6 and 7). Unfortunately, we
failed to further improve the reaction efficiency when other
reaction parameters, such as base additive, solvent and tem-
perature, were extensively examined (see the ESI, † for details).
With the optimized reaction conditions being established,
we then explored the substrate scope of the (4+1) annulation
and the results are summarized in Scheme 2. In general, these
reactions took place smoothly under the standard conditions
and aﬀorded cyclopentene products in moderate to good yields.
A wide range of 1,4-diphenyl-3-butenones 1a–1f with different
electron-bias phenyl ketone moieties were well tolerated.
Among them, substrates 1b and 1c bearing an electron-rich
phenyl group gave the corresponding products in relatively
higher yields than the ones with an electron-poor phenyl group
including substrates 1d–1f. These results indicated that the
rate-determining step might not involve the generation of
dienoate species. The yields of products 3g and 3l respectively
dropped to 50% and 61% likely due to the increased steric
hindrance. The reaction was also applicable to the substrates
bearing a heteroaryl ketone moiety, such as furan and thiophene.
The corresponding products3j and 3k were isolated in moderate
yields. Then, the effect of subst i t u e n to nt h ea l k e n em o i e t yw a s
briefly explored. Again, substrates1m and 1n bearing an electron-
rich phenyl group exhibited somewhat higher reactivity than
substrate1o. 1-Phenyl-3-butenone1p was also a suitable substrate
to deliver product 3p in 58% yield. In contrast to aryl ketone
substrates 1a–1q,m e t h y lk e t o n es u b s t r a t e1r showed much
less reactivity, affording product 3r only in 38% yield. Notably,
1-phenyl-1,5-hexadien-3-one1s readily reacted with allenoate 2,
giving product 3s with three distinct alkenes.
When the protocol was applied tob,g-unsaturatedN-acylpyrazole
1t,
9 it was surprising to isolate compound 4 in 30% yield while
the expected (4+1) annulation product was not observed at all
(Scheme 3).
10 Likely due to its much more acidicaH, N-acylpyrazole
1t could be rapidly deprotonated by zwitterion intermediate E
that was resulted from the addition of phosphine to allenoate 2.
Vinyl phosphonium intermediate F was thus generated, which
was responsible for the formation of product 4 via an umpolung
g-addition mechanism11 (Scheme 3).
These observations are against the previous reports
wherein intermediate E is generally believed to rapidly undergo

Although this unexpected result closely related to the unique
b,g-unsaturated N-acylpyrazole substrate may be a specific case,
it indeed provides a good clue to re-consider the chemical
behaviour of allenoate 2 under Lewis base catalysis.
10
(1)
More interestingly, the reaction of 1a and 2 with the use of
PtBu3 as a catalyst under the otherwise identical conditions
instead produced compound 5, clearly pointing out that a
reaction mechanism diﬀerent from the one leading to cyclo-
pentene would be involved (eqn (1) and Scheme 4).
12
Taking these results into account, a plausible mechanism
for the (4+1) annulation of 1a and 2 is depicted in Scheme 4.
Our previous studies supposed that both the g- and b0-positions
are available for nucleophilic attack, which lead to zwiterrionic
intermediates C (path a) and C
0 (path b), 12 respectively. Then,
the resulting dienoate D undergoes an intramolecular SN20-type
process to aﬀord product 3a and regenerate the phosphine
catalyst (path a). On the other hand, intermediate C0 may
undergo 1,2-elimination of the phosphine catalyst to produce
compound 5 (Scheme 4). We believed that the g-position of
intermediate B might become congested due to the presence of
aP tBu3 group, thus switching the attack of dienoate A from the
g-position to the b0-position to form C0 with high regioselec-
tivity (Scheme 4).
To check the practicality of the process, the reaction of 1g
and 2 was carried out in 2.0 mmol scale under the optimal
conditions, which gave product 3g in a synthetically useful yield
(57%). Moreover, product 3g could be converted into
spiro[4.4]nonane derivative 6 in 73% yield by using common
Heck reaction conditions, highlighting the applicability of this
protocol toward the synthesis of a structurally complex frame-
work (Scheme 5).
In summary, we have developed the phosphine-catalysed
(4+1) annulation of b
0-acetoxy allenoate and a b,g-unsaturated
carbonyl compound, which provides facile access to cyclopen-
tenes of synthetic value under mild conditions. In this process,
the b,g-unsaturated carbonyl compound serves as a aC,
aC-bisnucleophile and nicely matches the reactivity of the
involved diene-phosphonium species to accomplish (4+1) annula-
tion, which complements the well-known vinylogous g-addition
and a-addition of a b,g-unsaturated carbonyl compound. Further
investigation on the asymmetricversion of the (4+1) annulation is
underway and will be reported in due course.
